intro: Core question: why do some companies perform better than others?
Rumelt: diagnosis → guiding policy → coherent actions (e.g. Southwest Airlines).
Bad strategy: avoiding the problem, confusing goals with strategy, bad objectives, fluff.
Vision (why, C-level) → strategy (what, top management) → tactics (how, field).
Changing the rules of the game: Apple (blue ocean).
ext: External analysis: the firm chooses, the context does not. Three layers: macro (PESTEL), industry (5 forces), firm.
Four channels to profit: demand, costs, competition, rules.
PESTEL: prioritise by impact × predictability (plan, scenarios, monitor, set aside).
Five forces: entrants, suppliers, buyers, substitutes, rivalry; the stronger they are, the less profitable the industry.
SWOT: internal (strengths, weaknesses) vs external (opportunities, threats, from PESTEL and the 5 forces); useful only if it ends in a choice.
Uber: strong buyers and rivalry → unattractive industry; profit through scale and ecosystem; S+O option: demand platform for robotaxis.
Airline case: low cost (one aircraft type, point-to-point, fast turnarounds) = 47 years of Southwest profit; Covid: traffic -90%, resilience is a choice (cash, flexibility, options).
Intended strategy → realised and emergent strategy (levers: structure, systems, people).
int: External analysis: where is the profit? Internal analysis: who can capture it? Business-specific effects matter more than industry in the data cited.
Resources (what the firm owns) → capabilities (what it can do) → competitive advantage.
VRIO: Valuable, Rare, Imperfectly imitable, Organized to exploit. Parity ≠ temporary advantage ≠ sustained advantage; without O, unexploited advantage.
Imitation is slowed by history, causal ambiguity and social complexity. Dynamic capabilities: sense, seize, reconfigure.
Value chain: primary and support activities; Zara and Southwest win through a system of activities that reinforce each other.
Choosing a place: upstream/downstream integration, specialisation, control of a bottleneck. Margins along the chain are not directly comparable.
Consulting: six families; organised by industry × function × geography; pyramid model. Headcount/salary figures are approximate, dated and on different scopes.
Commercial due diligence = market/position (S2), operational = resources/capabilities (S3), completed by financial, legal and technical experts.
bls: Business strategy = 3 choices: who (which customers), what (which needs, which promise), how (which resources and activities). Choosing also means giving up.
Competitive advantage: create more value than rivals, as the customer perceives it. WTP €100, price €70, cost €50 → customer surplus €30, margin €20.

Two levers: lower cost (more margin, or lower price at equal margin) or raise willingness to pay (differentiation). The advantage exists only if customers see it (Bezos: the customer is a guest, we are the host).

Porter: 2 sources of advantage (cost, differentiation) × 2 scopes (broad market, narrow segment) = cost leadership (Ryanair, Lidl), differentiation (Apple, Zara), cost focus (Dacia, hotelF1), differentiation focus (Hermès, Ferrari).
Cost leadership: lowest cost for an acceptable product, price at market level; low cost is not low price. Sources: scale, learning, simplicity, cheap inputs.
Differentiation: the test is that the premium the customer pays exceeds the cost of the difference (Hermès: craft and scarcity; Zara: speed).
Focus: serve one segment better (risk: niche too small); hybrid (IKEA, Toyota): more value at moderate cost, possible with a strong system despite Porter's "stuck in the middle" warning.
Fit (Porter 1996): a position = a system of coherent activities + trade-offs (Ryanair: one aircraft, secondary airports, fast turnarounds, no connections). Without trade-offs, no position.
Each strategy answers the 5 forces differently: cost protects against price wars and powerful buyers; differentiation builds loyalty and makes offers incomparable.

Advantage cycle: build → exploit → imitate → erode → renew. Erosion by imitation, technology, low-end entrants, tastes. Responses: defend, extend, renew. Price advantages erode fast, culture-based ones slowly.

Fashion thread: four firms, one wardrobe. Operating margin: Hermès 41%, Inditex ≈20%, H&M 8%, Shein ≈4% (last full year; Hermès, H&M, Shein 2025, Inditex fiscal 2024). Each margin reflects a positioning choice.

Reading the positions: Primark and Ryanair = cost leadership; Hermès = differentiation focus; Apple = differentiation; Zara and IKEA = hybrids; Shein = cost + speed; H&M = debatable (cheaper than Zara? more fashionable than Primark?).
Why customers choose: only two levers: pay less (low price, no frills) or get more (quality, design, brand, speed, trust). Cost works on the first, differentiation on the second.
New market space ("blue ocean"): make competition irrelevant (Cirque du Soleil: theatre + circus); hard to repeat, easy to imitate once proven.
plt: 4-question reading method: which cost/barrier falls (5 forces) → where is durable value (VRIN) → which decision is forced (rivals) → which risk/trade-off. The object changes, not the method.

Schumpeter (1942): creative destruction: innovation replaces the old economy, it does not add to it. Christensen (1997): low-end disruption: a simple, cheaper offer wins the bottom of the market then moves up. Often both (Amazon started with books).
Internet: 4 costs fall to (almost) zero: search, copy, distribute, match (Goldfarb & Tucker, 2019) → easy entry, intermediaries lose their paid role.
Near-zero marginal cost: fixed cost is the barrier; scale pays (the biggest can price lowest); free becomes possible if a second payer exists (advertisers, other side).
Long tail (Anderson 2004): niches added up can rival hits; Elberse (2008) nuance: hits still carry a large share of revenue.
Pipeline (Zara) sells, platform (Vinted) connects: it owns the connection between the two sides, neither the item nor the sale. Most firms are hybrids (Zalando).
4 network effects: direct (messaging), cross-side (Airbnb hosts/travellers), negative (spam, congestion), local (ride-hailing per city). They raise the entry barrier but each has a limit.
Chicken-and-egg of a two-sided market: seed one side, subsidise, go local, do things that don't scale (Airbnb NY 2009: door-to-door photos, revenue ×2).
Who pays = a strategic choice: monetise the side that values the transaction most (Vinted: buyers pay, sellers free); this decides which side to attract first.
4 platform risks: leakage (dealing outside), quality/moderation (central cost), regulation (DMA 2022/1925 applicable since 2023, session 7), dependence on one player's rules.

Models: free funded by ads (Amazon ads $68.6bn in 2025, launched 2012); sell the outcome not the product (Rolls-Royce Power-by-the-Hour, 1962); subscription = initial revenue dip, pays only if customers stay (Adobe: revenue -7.9% in 2013 while subscription +69%).
SaaS: ARR = MRR × 12; NRR > 100% = growth without new customers; churn = losses that cost years; Rule of 40 = growth + margin (30% + 15% = 45).
Amazon 2025: AWS = 18% of net sales ($716.9bn) but 57% of operating income ($80bn): the most visible business is not the profit engine; strategy is the portfolio.
ma: Corporate strategy: which businesses to be in, which stages of the value chain, which countries; M&A moves a boundary, and selling a business is also a strategic choice.
An acquisition is an action, not a strategy (Rumelt): for each deal ask which diagnosis it answers and why buy rather than build or ally (borrow).

5 reasons to buy tied to course tools: scale → 5 forces (Vusion-Pricer); control of a stage → value chain (Amazon-Whole Foods); capability → VRIO (Facebook-Instagram, Vusion-Memory); enter a market → entry barriers (Walmart-Jet.com); transform → corporate (Microsoft-Nokia, failure).

Build: full control and its culture, but slow (choose if you have the skills and time). Borrow: speed and shared risk, but dependence (if access is enough). Buy: speed + control, but premium and integration risk (if control is needed and integration possible). Capron & Mitchell (2012).
Organic vs acquisition: organic costs no premium but takes years; acquisition brings customers, team and know-how at once at the price of a premium and a culture merger.
Cited M&A failure rate: 70-90% (Christensen et al., HBR 2011); 12 cents lost per dollar spent at announcement (1998-2001, Moeller et al.). The seller usually captures the premium.
Value for the buyer = synergies - premium - integration costs. Cost synergies are often delivered, revenue synergies often disappoint; winner's curse in auctions.
Failure factors: overpaying, overestimated synergies, culture clash, slow integration, distraction from the core, ignored regulators. Failures are decided before signing or in the first 100 days.
Strategic buyer (synergies, pays cash or shares, can pay more) vs financial buyer (return then resale, cash often with debt, founders often kept).

3 valuation methods: comparables (multiple × metric, depends on the market), precedent transactions (include control premium, e.g. Pricer +29.6%), DCF (sensitive to assumptions). EV - net debt = equity value. Maximum price = standalone value + synergies actually capturable.
Divestment in 6 steps: prepare → approach → first offers → due diligence → signing → closing. Dual track: sale and fundraising in parallel to test price and keep a fallback.
Price is also terms: earn-out and warranties (private), premium and fairness opinion (listed), carve-out, LBO, stock merger (who controls?).

After closing: prepare → reassure (day 1) → organise (100 days) → integrate (years 1-3). Degrees of integration (Haspeslagh & Jemison): absorption, symbiosis, holding, preservation, depending on need for resource sharing × need for autonomy.

M&A follows the cost of money: record 2021 ($6.8tn), trough 2022-23, record megadeals in 2025 (68 deals > $10bn). In 2024 buyers sought savings (59% scale), in 2025 growth and capabilities (60% scope), per Bain.

cadre: Marketing = identify (or create), acquire and keep customers, profitably.
Model = stylised representation of reality, built for a specific purpose.
Response model: links a marketing effort to sales (S-curve between a minimum and a maximum).
Allocating a budget in proportion to market share ignores the marginal response to spending.
No model is true, some are useful: 50% data, 50% manager.
seg: Good segment: distinct, homogeneous, identifiable, substantial, useful.
Bases = why segments differ (needs, benefits). Descriptors = who they are and how to reach them (age, income, media).
Form segments on bases, never on descriptors.
Dendrogram: cut before the big jump. Scree plot: look for the elbow.
Discriminant analysis: predict the segment from descriptors; hit rate = correctly classified / total.
conj: Product = bundle of attribute levels; utility = sum of partworths (0-100 scale).
Attribute importance = gap between its best and worst partworth.
Estimation: regression of ratings on 0/1 variables; choice-based conjoint uses a binary regression.
Choice rules: first choice (house), share of preference (meal), logit (clothing), alpha-rule (known shares).
Design: 4 to 6 attributes, 2 to 4 levels, no correlated attributes.
Simulations: new product, new entrant, cannibalisation, niches.
pos: Perceptual map: close = strong competition, on dimensions relevant to customers.
Vectors: same direction = correlated; opposite = negatively correlated; 90° = independent; far from origin = significant.
Orthogonal projection to rank brands on an attribute.
Perceptions matter more than reality (Volvo, the drill, Débitel); wishful marketing is a "death wish".
The map is relative; the analyst interprets the axes.
Add preferences: a distinctive position may interest nobody.
price: Value salami: created value lies between the seller's minimum price and the buyer's maximum price; the price shares it.
Strategies: cost, competition, demand, value, discrimination.
Value-in-use = costs the product saves the customer (seals: $35).
Discrimination: different prices by reservation price; limits: arbitrage, legality, feeling of unfairness.
Gabor-Granger: purchase intent at randomly shown prices → optimal price; interpolate, don't extrapolate.
Van Westendorp: psychological optimum = crossing of "too cheap" × "too expensive".
score: Choice-based segmentation: group by probability of response, not similarity of needs.
CART: successive splits on the best predictor (Gini, entropy); needs lots of data; risk of overfitting.
Marginal impact of an action is maximal at p = 50%.
Trigger a purchase → target the most likely; influence a behaviour → target the undecided.
Score = probability × expected amount; score classes A to D.
resalloc: Resource = valuable (productive) AND available in limited quantity: budget, salespeople, time, R&D.
Two questions: size the optimal level of investment, then allocate that budget across options.
Sizing: % of sales (inertia), competitor benchmark, or ROI optimisation, the best one but it requires the response function.
Response function: sales as a function of effort (diminishing returns); the optimal budget maximises profit, not sales.
A specific response function per market / segment / region (different customers, potentials, competition).
Estimation: historical data (variability?), experiments (costly, risky), managerial judgement (fast, consensual).
Delphi: expert panel, 2+ questionnaire rounds, anonymous synthesis by a facilitator, revisions, convergence to mean/median.
Calibration: Y0 (no visits), Y1 (unchanged), Y2 (+50%), Y3 (maximum) → AdBudg curve: a = saturation, b = minimum sales, d = competition/noise.
No consensus: test several estimates; if the result changes, the point is critical → more data needed.
20-salespeople study: +11.9% (with recommendations) vs +3.8% (control); +8.1 pts, p < .025; ~half a day per salesperson.
synth: Which offer to launch? → conjoint analysis.
At what price? → Gabor-Granger, Van Westendorp, conjoint.
Whom to target? → CART, logit, scoring.
Where to put my media budget? → response models, MMM.

title.dm: IS strategy and Digital Matrix (13 Oct)

it.eval: Written paper final exam: 45% (Tuesday 8 December, 16:30-17:30, time confirmed on the course Moodle page; true/false, MCQ and open questions; 2-page cheat sheet allowed). In-class group work: 30%. Oral participation: 25%. Attendance compulsory.

dt: Managing IS (strategy, projects, suppliers) vs managing through IS (analytics, platforms, AI).
Landmarks: TCP/IP (1974), Web (CERN, 1989, public in 1993), Minitel, iPhone (9 January 2007), GAFAM and BATX.
COBOL: 70 to 80% of active code of critical systems, 95% of card and ATM transactions.
dm: IS = technology + tasks + people; strategy = where to go and how (Pearlson and Saunders).
Digital transformation = integration of SMACIT across the whole firm; a managerial problem before a technical one.
Competitive advantage: Barney (1991), Porter (1985); Porter's 5 forces, IT acts on each.
Digital Matrix (Venkatraman): incumbents, tech entrepreneurs, digital giants × edge, core, root.
Rules Matrix: orchestrate and participate, co-creation of capabilities, amplify human talent with machines.
cloud: IS outsourcing = paying a vendor to perform one's IS activities; scopes: operations, applications, support, business processes.
For: costs, core business, access to tech/talent, flexibility. Against: dependence, transaction costs, loss of control, slower innovation.
Three deals: traditional outsourcing, transformation outsourcing (BPM), strategic cloud/AI agreements (not necessarily strict outsourcing).
Outsourcing/insourcing = boundaries of the firm; offshore/nearshore = geography. Sacem case: external audit as a lever, floodable server room, SALMA project (professional host, €717K + €330K/yr).
Cloud: pay-per-use billing, web access, customisation by configuration, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS layers.
Success: sophistication of the sourcing decision, of the selection (RFI → short list → RFP, joint business+IT evaluation), and contractual (SLA) + relational governance.
proj: Project management = final deliverable + finite duration and budget (vs ongoing management).
Waterfall: good for fixed scope and requirements, heavy documentation; weak against discoveries along the way (overplanning, knowing before having seen).

Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change: principles → methods (Scrum, DevOps, XP) → practices (user stories, meetings, prototyping).
Scrum artifacts: product backlog (all requirements as user stories), sprint backlog (selection + plan, task board), increment = working software at each sprint end.
User story: "As a <role>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>" + optional acceptance criteria.
Roles: Product Owner (vision, backlog, priorities, acceptance criteria), Development Team (≤ ~10, cross-functional, autonomous), Scrum Master (process coach).
Meetings: sprint planning, daily Scrum, sprint review, retrospective; sprint of 2 to 4 weeks.
Agile is no miracle: depends on context; ambidexterity between efficiency/innovation, standardisation/differentiation, stability/agility, control/autonomy.
Enterprise IS = large software supporting processes, information flows, reporting and analytics; 3 families: ERP, SCM, CRM.
ERP: integrated database, industry best practices, tracks resources / processes / structure / data (e.g. SAP S/4HANA).
SCM: buying-making-moving, network of suppliers-manufacturer-distributors-customers, reduces lead times and inventory.
CRM: unified customer view, satisfaction and loyalty; operational, analytical, communicative components (e.g. Salesforce).
5 recommendations for an ERP: management sponsorship, external experts, user training, multidisciplinary approach, incremental implementation.
data: Analytics = analysis of data with mathematical techniques to inform or improve decisions. 3 types: descriptive (what happened; aggregation, data mining), predictive (what will happen; statistical models, e.g. credit scores), prescriptive (what to do; optimisation and scenario simulation).
3 Vs of big data: Volume (mega/gigabytes), Velocity (real time, hourly, daily, monthly), Variety (text, click stream, audio, video).

Benefits of analytics: efficiency and productivity (operational), faster and better decisions (tactical), better financial performance (strategic). Data can also be monetised and sold ("pay for attention" model).
cyber: Cyber-resilience: anticipate, resist, recover, adapt, beyond prevention alone, which is never perfect.
4 categories of cybercrime: individuals, property (digital assets), organisations and governments, society.
Cybercrime: $8.15 trillion in 2023 → $10.5 trillion expected in 2025; France $93.46bn; 69% companies, 20% local authorities, 11% healthcare (2023).
"Microsoft bug" of 19 July 2024 = CrowdStrike Falcon Sensor update; ≈ $5.4bn for the Fortune 500 (Parametrix).
Y2K: COBOL dates in YYMMDD, $300-600bn; Blayais (27 Dec 1999): one event can defeat several supposedly independent protections.
GDPR (2018), AI Act (2025, risk-based), DSA (2023), Data Act/DGA (2023), DMA (2024, gatekeepers).
NIS-2 (2022): ≈ 160,000 entities, notification within 24 h, fines up to €10M or 2% of global turnover; CER (2022/2024, 10 sectors); DORA (17 Jan 2025, finance).
French SNR (April 2022, SGDSN); OFAC (Nov 2023, police - cybercrime); ARIANE (2026, DINUM + DITP - State IS).
plat: 3 laws of the digital economy: Metcalfe's law (V ∝ N², direct and indirect network effects → winner-takes-all/most); zero marginal cost (1st copy $100M, the 10 millionth $0 → infinite scalability); high switching costs and lock-in (Apple iOS ecosystem, Microsoft 365 stack).

Market cap shift: 2005 world top 10 = oil/banking/industry → today Big Tech and AI infrastructure; tech accounts for more than 80% of S&P 500 value creation over 10 years; asset-light giants earn a better ROIC than industrials.

Attention economy: attention drives value (Herbert Simon: "a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention"); algorithmic signals (likes, shares, watch time) ⇒ monetisation (Meta, Alphabet; data as raw material).

Dominant models: advertising/AdTech (free services monetising behaviour), subscription/SaaS (perpetual licence → recurring revenue ARR/MRR, gross margin > 80%), IaaS (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud = "tollbooths" of digital infrastructure; AWS = majority of Amazon's operating profit).
Multi-sided platforms: connect buyers/sellers, creators/viewers, drivers/passengers (Uber, Airbnb, App Store) and take 15 to 30% take-rate for trust, discovery and payment rails.

Tesla case: the vehicle becomes a "computer on wheels"; software, connectivity and battery = 50-60% of the value of new-generation cars; traditional auto margins 5-8% vs software 70%+; software features (FSD) create lifetime customer value after the sale.

Physical bottlenecks: ASML = global monopoly (100%) on EUV lithography; TSMC makes > 90% of the most advanced chips; Nvidia = monopoly on AI GPUs; data centres and energy = new bottlenecks of the 2020s.

Course summary: dominance goes to zero-marginal-cost assets; network effects produce winner-takes-all; value migrates to software and cloud; tech chains have critical single-point-of-failure bottlenecks.
reg: Cyber-regulation = regulating cyberspace ("cyber" from cybernetics, Norbert Wiener 1948). It must be regulated because it combines technology, economy, power, regulation and society, and raises political stakes: economic and information power, surveillance, cybersecurity, cyberwar, free speech, digital sovereignty.

History: US antitrust against Microsoft (1990s-2001), then the EU sanctions giants through competition law (Microsoft €497M in 2004 and €561M in 2013; Google Shopping €2.42bn in 2017; Android €4.34bn in 2018; AdSense €1.49bn in 2019). Limit: a fine is not the restoration of competition.

From punitive to ex ante rules: the DMA sets obligations on gatekeepers before any abuse is proven (classic antitrust asks whether the law was broken). Initial gatekeepers: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta, Microsoft. DMA fines: Apple €500M (anti-steering) and Meta €200M ("consent or pay"), 23 April 2025; Google €460M + €430M (23 July 2026).

GDPR (2016, applied 2018): consent, purpose limitation, minimisation, rights of access/rectification/erasure, DPO, breach notification, fines up to €20M or 4% of global turnover. DSA (2022, applied 2024): algorithmic transparency, risk assessments, VLOP audits, protection of minors. DMA (2022, applied 2023): no self-preferencing, open APIs, side-loading, portability; fines up to 10% of turnover (20% for repeat).

NIS-2 (2022, applied 2024): critical infrastructure (energy, health, finance, transport, cloud, data centres); incident notification within 24 h, supply-chain risk, fines up to €10M or 2% of turnover; about 160,000 entities. DORA (applicable 17 Jan 2025): operational resilience of the financial sector (ICT risk, incidents, resilience testing, third parties, continuity). MiCA (Dec 2024): crypto-assets, ART vs EMT.

AI Act (2024, phased application from 2025): 4 risk levels: minimal (anti-spam), limited (chatbots, transparency), high (recruitment, credit scoring, strict rules), unacceptable (social scoring, banned). CRA (2024, obligations from 2026): mandatory cybersecurity of digital products, vulnerability reporting, security updates; fines up to €15M or 2.5% of turnover. Data Act (2023, applicable 2025): access to connected-device data, cloud switching without fees from 2027.

Others: Copyright directive (2019, article 17: proactive monitoring, press neighbouring right); right to repair (2024, USB-C, update transparency, against planned obsolescence); eIDAS 2 (2024, European digital identity wallet by end 2026); under discussion in November 2026: Digital Omnibus, Cybersecurity Act 2, Digital Networks Act, business wallets, CSAM regulation.

United States: USA PATRIOT Act (2001, expands investigative powers, not unlimited access to data); FISA 702 (foreign intelligence targeting non-Americans located outside the US, under conditions); CLOUD Act (2018, US providers may have to produce data even if stored abroad, under legal process). Geopolitical tension: Trump tariff threats (25 August 2025) against digital rules.

Takeaways: (1) cyber-regulation aims to frame cyberspace in all its dimensions; (2) the EU has produced many texts in 20 years; (3) its limits are geopolitical, legal and linked to innovation. In-class case: 2-page memo to an investor, identifying the EU/US texts that apply, explaining why they apply or not, and ending with a clear recommendation.
